sheets.name: Read_me
rows: RIVERKNOLL RENEWAL | MATERIAL LIST v2, matched to the design (Nov 26 2026)

The design is model v24: 18 rows of 10 attached units, 12 two-story rows of 4-bed townhomes and 6 three-story rows of 6-bed townhomes, each row with 2 single-level accessible end units, 744 beds. Every wall is System 3E perlite block, upper floors are concrete plank, roofs are wood trusses. Everything but the System 3E blocks comes from suppliers within a couple of miles (Local_Suppliers).

Rule for v2: the list holds what the design calls for, nothing more and nothing less. Each line says what in the design calls for it. Where the design doesn't set something yet, the quantity is yellow on Inputs and listed on Design_Check.
Building cost, whole project: $49.0M, $162 a SF, $65,885 a bed (low $97, high $258 a SF).
All in, with model v24's own site, design, contingency, inflation and financing: $96.8M, $320 a SF, $130,049 a bed (low $79,118, high $205,217 a bed).
Model v24, unchanged: $176.96M, $305 a SF building, $595 all in, $237,854 a bed. Check_vs_Model explains the gap.

Sheets: Inputs; Townhome_4bed_2story; Townhome_6bed_3story (new); Accessible_End_Unit; Row_2story; Row_3story (new); Project_Total (new); Design_Check (what changed and what the design doesn't set); Check_vs_Model; Local_Suppliers; Sources.
Unit costs are installed prices (material plus trade labor), national cost guides 2025-26, not Rochester bids. Orange unit cost = my estimate with no source yet. Material list v1 is kept unchanged.

sheets.name: Design_Check
rows: DOES THE LIST MATCH THE DESIGN? What changed from v1, and what the design does not set yet

Model v24 builds 6 three-story rows of 6-bed townhomes (312 of the 744 beds). v1 listed only the two-story row, so 42% of the beds had no materials. v2 adds a 6-bed townhome list, a three-story row and a whole-project total.

Moved from the home lists to the row sheets: 7 full-height walls between townhomes and 2 one-story walls at the end units, per row. Same total in a two-story row; in a three-story row v1's way would have counted 288 SF too many.
Side walls next to the end units

Above the end units, the side walls of townhomes 1 and 8 are outside walls. v1 priced them at half a wall plus render; v2 prices the full wall. Also adds the short stub where the 36.8 ft deep end unit runs past the 32 ft townhome, and its footing.

v1 insulated the whole slab. The NY 2025 energy code asks for R-10 at the slab edge, 4 ft deep (Insulation Institute N112). Side edges sit between heated homes. v2 insulates the front and back edges only and adds the vapor retarder the code asks for under every slab.
The plank is the ceiling of the floor below, so it needs a skim coat of plaster, not hung drywall. Drywall stays only on the top-floor ceiling under the roof trusses.
The v23 finding (air sealing to 1.5 ACH50 with a blower-door test, about $1,200 a home, pays back in about 14 years) was in the model but not in the list.
Low-slope roof on the three-story rows
Model v24 gives the three-story rows a low-slope roof to stay under 35 ft. v2 prices a TPO membrane with R-30 above the deck (the code line for that roof), not shingles.
One flight per floor above the first: 1 in a two-story home, 2 in a three-story home.

Windows (8), interior doors (8) and closets now come from the design in model v24, not from today's Riverknoll units. The organizer's counts (4 windows, 5 interior doors, 1 closet) describe today's 3-bedroom units; a new 4-bed needs an egress window in every bedroom (IRC R310).

Everything else: System 3E blocks for every wall, plank upper floors, wood roof trusses, render outside, plaster inside, no siding, sheathing, house wrap or wall insulation, attic R-49 (the NY 2025 ceiling line), unit prices and sources.

sheets.name: Check_vs_Model
rows: WHY THIS LIST COMES TO ABOUT HALF OF MODEL v24
This list, whole project, building cost: $162 a SF at mid (low $97, high $258). Model v24: $305 a SF (two-story row).

1. The two numbers are built in different ways. The model starts from $300 a SF taken from student housing projects and benchmarks (APX $200-$325 off-campus, SUNY cost per bed, the Lodge and Apex), then adjusts it for the row shape and System 3E. It never adds up materials. This list adds up each material and trade, quantity by quantity.

2. The list's unit prices are national homeowner cost guides (HomeGuide, Angi and others). A Rochester commercial contractor bidding 18 rows would price labor, supervision and risk higher than a guide written for one homeowner.
3. NY prevailing wage could apply if public money pays 30% or more of a project over $5M (NY Labor Law 224-a). That would raise labor cost a lot. A lawyer should confirm.

4. Not in the list's 15% contractor line: permits, temporary power and heat, winter work, dumpsters, cleaning, insurance and bonds, testing and punch list. A commercial general contractor's general conditions often run well above 15% on their own.
5. The national benchmarks sit near the list, not the model: NAHB 2024 $162 a SF (builder cost before overhead and profit) and ICC Feb 2026 $175.92 for a wood-frame R-3 home.

6. What it means: the list is the floor of what the materials and trades cost; the model is the conservative institutional number. Model v24 stays at $305 until a Rochester contractor prices these lists. That bid is the only thing that settles it.
